title: Cause, Effect & Conditions
pedagogicalStatus: Unreviewed draft: formative practice only; CEFR mastery disabled.

sources.title: Ideal resistor in a virtual circuit (reading; practice)
paragraphs: A computer model shows an ideal 10 Ω resistor. The resistance stays the same. When the model applies 2 V, the current is 0.20 A. When it applies 4 V, the current is 0.40 A. The current increases because the voltage increases while resistance stays constant. The group records these model values in a table. They do not connect a real electrical supply.

sources.title: A virtual cart moving at a steady speed (reading; practice)
paragraphs: A virtual cart travels along a straight line at 2 meters per second. It travels 2 meters in one second and 6 meters in three seconds. Because its speed is constant, the distance increases by 2 meters each second. If the cart continues at the same speed for another two seconds, it will travel another 4 meters. These are computer-model values, not measurements of a real cart.

sources.title: Cooling model and room temperature (reading; practice)
paragraphs: A simple model shows an object at 35 °C in a room at 20 °C. After five minutes, the displayed temperature is 30 °C. The model shows the object cooling because it is warmer than the room. The student predicts that it will continue to cool if the same model conditions continue. The reading does not tell us its exact temperature after another five minutes. All values are simulated.

sources.title: Study habits and understanding a graph (reading; practice)
paragraphs: A physics student does not understand the axes on a graph, so she asks her instructor for help. If the horizontal axis shows time, she will label it “Time (s).” Her instructor explains that a label needs a quantity and a unit. After the explanation, the student corrects the axis label. This is a learning example, not an experiment.

items.prompt: Complete: “The current increased ___ the voltage increased.”
items.feedback: Because introduces the reason; so introduces the result. With the same reason/result pair, their sentence order changes. Avoid “because ... so” as two connectors for one ordinary cause–effect relation.

items.prompt: Complete: “The voltage increased, ___ the model current increased.”
items.feedback: Because introduces the reason; so introduces the result. With the same reason/result pair, their sentence order changes. Avoid “because ... so” as two connectors for one ordinary cause–effect relation.

items.prompt: Choose the sentence that gives a reason.
accepted: The cart traveled farther because it moved for more time.
items.feedback: Because introduces the reason; so introduces the result. With the same reason/result pair, their sentence order changes. Avoid “because ... so” as two connectors for one ordinary cause–effect relation.
options: The cart traveled farther because it moved for more time.
The cart traveled farther so it moved for more time.

options: The resistor stayed at 10 Ω, so the current rose when voltage rose.
The resistor stayed at 10 Ω because the current rose when voltage rose.
